title: Bladder cancer mistaken for UTI, perimenopause in women
text:
Four years.

That is how much time passed between when Andrea Harris first presented to her GP with a suspected bladder infection, and when she was diagnosed with advanced, muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

Ms Harris went back to the doctor multiple times over these four years, wanting to understand more about the root cause of her symptoms.

At one stage, Ms Harris recalls being "in tears" in the doctor's office, pressing for more extensive testing.

Cancer patients 'completely blindsided' by out-of-pocket expenses A report investigating the financial and legal impact of cancer in Victoria has found both patients and carers have significant out-of-pocket costs.

"I'd have a seven-day lot of antibiotics, and I'd be good for six or seven weeks and then I'd start to get symptoms again," she said.

By the time she was finally diagnosed in March 2024, Ms Harris's cancer had advanced to stage three.

In Australia, three in four people diagnosed with bladder cancer are men, but experts are concerned about the number of women, like Ms Harris, presenting with late-stage bladder cancer.

Alison Zhang, a medical oncologist at Macquarie University Hospital, said although bladder cancer symptoms, like blood in the urine and a frequent need to wee, were similar in both sexes, they were easy to misdiagnose as urinary tract infections (UTIs) or perimenopause in women.

Alison Zhang wants to improve outcomes for women diagnosed with bladder cancer. (Supplied: Alison Zhang)

Bladder cancer in Australia

About 3,345 cases of bladder cancer were estimated to be diagnosed in Australia last year.

But unlike most other cancers, the five-year survival rate has dropped since 1987.

Women diagnosed with bladder cancer in Australia face about a 50 per cent chance of living five years post-diagnosis, while men have an almost 60 per cent chance.

"Women tend to present later with later-stage disease, which is a real problem," Dr Zhang said.

Magdalena Simonis, a practising GP and women's health expert from the University of Melbourne, said men often had their bladder cancer symptoms — especially blood in the urine — escalated quickly as UTIs were far less common in men, and therefore unlikely to be the cause.

"If a man shows up with microscopic, that is, invisible blood in the urine, or visible blood in the urine, we would immediately advance that person to further investigations," she said.

"When a woman presents with the symptoms of bladder cancer, the symptoms are not dissimilar to those of a UTI; they might have a burning sensation with urination or blood in their urine."

Christine La Rose, a patient and support lead for advocacy group BEAT Bladder Cancer Australia, said there needed to be "more focus, more urgency and awareness" on improving outcomes for women.

An otherwise fit and healthy Christine La Rose was shocked to be diagnosed with bladder cancer at 49. (Supplied: Christine La Rose)

Ms La Rose, a bladder cancer survivor herself, faced a short diagnostic delay after initially being told the blood in her urine had been caused by a UTI.

"Blood in the urine should never be ignored; it should always be investigated," she said.

Other common symptoms of bladder cancer include a sudden change in urine colour, loss of appetite and weight loss.

Need for better referral pathways

There are a few things that experts agree will help improve outcomes for women.

The first, Dr Zhang said, was to increase community awareness about the symptoms of bladder cancer.

The 'taboo' cancer side effects we don't talk about Shame and stigma mean gynaecological side-effects from cancer treatment — affecting women's sexual, urinary and reproductive health — are under-reported and under-researched.

The second, Dr Simonis said, was that women who presented with recurrent UTIs — more than two within six months or three within a year — needed their symptoms investigated further with additional testing and/or a referral to a urologist.

"Women have traditionally been dismissed if they've got pain or ongoing symptoms," she said.

"Any level of discomfort that is continuous is something that we shouldn't really put up with."

Dr Simonis said GPs needed to consider risk factors of bladder disease, such as smoking and age, when treating female patients presenting with UTI-like symptoms.

"If they're a smoker, and they've got ongoing symptoms and recurrent symptoms, then alarm bells should ring a lot earlier," she said.

Ms La Rose said although bladder cancer was "traditionally seen as an older man's disease", she had met women in their 20s, 30s and 40s who had been diagnosed with it.

"You know your body best. If something doesn't feel right, go get it checked out," she said.

"Go back or go and get a second opinion. You really need to advocate for yourself and push for answers."

Margaret Blake was one of the many Australian women who needed to do just that.

Margaret Blake urges women to take bladder changes seriously and speak to a doctor as soon as possible. (Supplied: Margaret Blake)

Ms Blake saw three different GPs within the space of six months, concerned about her frequent need to urinate and finding blood in her urine.

She said her third GP was the first one to take her symptoms seriously, referring her for a series of tests, which eventually led to her bladder cancer diagnosis.

Survivors Ms Harris, Ms La Rose and Ms Blake all live with the ongoing consequences of treatment.

Ms La Rose has a neo-bladder, built by a surgeon using a piece of her intestine, which she is grateful to be able to empty easily and maintains a good quality of life.

"I'm really lucky. And I also know how lucky I am to still be here, given the diagnosis," she said.

" I know that if I'd waited any longer, the outcome could have been much much worse. "

title: Old Bendigo gold mine hosts underground piano concert
text:
A unique piano concert 61 metres underground in an old gold mine.

That was the brainwave of Bendigo Fine Music chair Thomas Heywood.

And yesterday that brainwave became reality, with a piano descending into the Central Deborah Gold Mine in Bendigo for a one-off evening performance.

The 300kg piano was formerly owned by Mr Heywood's mother, who was a renowned concert pianist.

"It's one of those classic 'don't drop the piano' scenarios," Mr Heywood said.

"We couldn't find any evidence that this has been done before.

"It's really quite emotional; it sounds fantastic in here. It is an amazing room for sound. There's a timber ceiling and hardstone walls, and they're ideal for musical performance."

Thomas Heywood came up with the idea of holding the concert in a gold mine to mark 175 years since gold was discovered in Bendigo. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

The Bendigo Fine Music event celebrated 175 years since gold was first discovered in the central Victorian city.

"In 1851, it changed our wonderful country forever," Mr Heywood said.

"We were always taught in school that basically the riches that followed from gold made possible what would have taken 500 years in European history to be achieved in a mere 50 years to Federation."

Friday's concert was limited to 60 attendees, who were allowed to remove their hard hats once in the concert room.

Pianist Yasmin Rowe said performing this rare and unusual concert was exciting.

"I've never played underground before, and this is just so special. When I entered this room, I thought it was so, so beautiful," Ms Rowe said.

"You've got this millions-of-years-old rock there right behind the piano; the light, the colour, the atmosphere is wonderful."

Yasmin Rowe and Ian Munro played before an audience of 60 people. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

Ms Rowe and fellow pianist Ian Munro said the underground concert made playing the piano interesting again.

" It's quite a dry acoustic. We have to adjust in real time, so using less pedal cause it's quite reverberant. "

Mr Munro said the rare and unusual concert brought back the memory of a conversation with his piano teacher at the age of 14, who questioned whether he would continue to love playing the piano as an adult.

"When I was 30 [and still loved playing piano], and now I'm very much older than 30, I'm still very interested; it's still got that magic for me."

The main body of the piano was covered with a blanket to protect from moisture in the tunnels. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

The operation to get the instrument underground was a family affair by Joshua McPherson, his wife Jo and son Sam.

Mr McPherson said it was "definitely the most unusual" place he had ever taken a piano.

The disassembled instrument was wheeled on a trolley into a lift and rolled along the rocky tunnels of the mine.

"We were worried about moisture dropping from the ceiling — that was our main concern. [It was] a little bit rough underfoot but nothing scary really," he said.

Nic Hamilton was tasked with making sure the piano stayed in tune. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Once in place, it was over to piano technician Nic Hamilton to ensure nothing had gone awry on the journey and to tune the piano before the concert.

"It's on the humid side but it takes some hours, perhaps even overnight to seep into the piano and cause any problems," he said.

"It's a fun thing to do, and it's very typical of Thomas [Heywood] to come up with projects that are interesting and exciting."

The piano is moved into the entrance to Central Deborah Gold Mine. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

title: Hanson takes aim at Coalition in fiery pitch to conservative voters
text:
Pauline Hanson has used a speech at a conservative conference to urge voters to abandon the Coalition, while acknowledging she would work with them if it meant removing Labor from government.

In a speech to the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in Brisbane, the One Nation leader described Opposition Leader Angus Taylor as a "smarmy management consultant" and said the Liberal Party was responsible for Australia's climate change commitments.

Loading

"The Liberals signed us up to Paris and net zero. The Liberals legislated the safeguard mechanism, and Labor locked the targets into law and made them even worse," she said.

"They signed us up to this mess, so why would we trust them to get us out of it?"

Ms Hanson pledged to hold a royal commission into net zero climate targets, should One Nation be elected.

Angus Taylor tries to find his place on the migration middle road As the three-cornered migration battle continues, Angus Taylor is trying to position his party in the middle of the government and One Nation.

And she further criticised the Coalition for creating the office of the eSafety Commissioner, a position she has pledged to abolish on the grounds it infringes on free speech online.

Both Ms Hanson and Mr Taylor addressed CPAC — a spin-off of conservative conferences held in the US and UK — on Saturday morning, taking aim at the Albanese government and pitching themselves as the conservative alternative.

It was the first time a Coalition leader has addressed the annual forum, although notable Liberal figures like Tony Abbott and Jacinta Nampijinpa Price have addressed it in recent years.

Jacinta Nampijinpa Price speaking at CPAC. (ABC: Luke Bowden)

But while Senator Hanson sharply criticised the Coalition, Mr Taylor made almost no mention of One Nation.

His speech made just one apparent indirect reference to Senator Hanson, referencing her dominance of the One Nation party and brand.

"Good government isn't built around one figure. You need a strong team," he said.

And he opened the speech by referencing a number of "mistakes" the Coalition made in government, acknowledging to the audience that "some of you may have doubts".

He pointed to areas like immigration policy, climate change and government spending during the pandemic as policy failures under Coalition governments.

Angus Taylor speaking at CPAC in Brisbane. (ABC : Luke Bowden )

"We made the mistake as a government of signing up to net zero," he said.

"Your frustrations about where we let you down in the recent past are understandable and reasonable. Believe me, I share them."

Both leaders reserved their strongest attacks for the Albanese government — Mr Taylor arguing it was leaving Australians "poorer, weaker, and demoralised", and Senator Hanson calling it "wretched and corrupt".

Hanson says ON would work with Coalition

Despite her strong rhetoric on the Coalition, Senator Hanson made clear that One Nation would work with them if it meant changing the government.

"One Nation will work with the Liberals and Nationals to remove this horrible Labor government and deliver something better," she said.

"That's what you, the people, want. It's the will of the people."

Matt Canavan in a Q&A with Pauline Hanson. (By Luke Bowden)

She referenced her time in prison after a 2003 conviction for electoral fraud, later quashed on appeal, under the Howard government, but said she would put "personal grievances aside".

"Yes, I do have reasons to hold a grudge, but I also have children and grandchildren," she said.

"Their futures and your futures matter more."

In a later speech, Nationals leader Matt Canavan also struck a more conciliatory tone, urging those on the right of politics not to become caught up fighting among themselves.

"My message to you today is, look, we do wear lots of different colours. I get that," he said.

"There's lots of different people here.

"But the one thing we have to do at the next election is all put the Labor Party last. That's what we've got to do."

title: SA starts Shield defence with innings win over Victoria
text:
South Australia has started its Sheffield Shield campaign in the same way it ended the last one, beating Victoria at Junction Oval.

The two-time defending champions wrapped up their dominating start today, beating the home side by an innings and 40 runs.

Fittingly, debutant Noah McFadyen took the last wicket of the game when he had David Moody caught and bowled, after top-scoring with 134 in SA's innings.

McFadyen had hit two sixes to go from 88 to 100, finished with 16 fours and five maximums.

The 23-year-old all-rounder had match figures of 3-65, including Moody's wicket to clinch the game.

Resuming at 7-175 and needing another 89 to bat again, Victoria was dismissed for 224.

Victoria made 244 in its first innings and SA took the game away from them with 508.

Fergus O'Neill top-scored in Victoria's second innings with 62, while Nathan McAndrew and Henry Thornton took three wickets apiece.

AAP/ABC

title: Champion golfer reflects on lasting legacy in outback WA
text:
Australian golfing champion Graham Marsh has built almost as many golf courses as the 70 tournament wins he collected over a decorated career.

At last count, it was 65 projects around the world as a golf course architect since 1986, including Secret Harbour, Terrey Hills and The Vines.

Despite turning 82 this year, Marsh's diary remains full, with projects in Queensland and Cyprus.

It was a full-circle moment for Marsh this week when he returned to his birthplace of Kalgoorlie for the WA PGA Championship, getting his hands on a trophy he won in 1978.

While his family left the historic mining city when he was an infant, Marsh's role as the architect of the Kalgoorlie Golf Course has left a lasting legacy.

Graham Marsh has returned to his birthplace at Kalgoorlie for the WA PGA Championship and (inset) in his playing days. (Main image: Jarrod Lucas, ABC Goldfields. Inset: State Library of WA)

"We don't have this desert form of golf in Australia, this is the first of its kind, and I think that makes it very special," he said.

"There have been attempts, there was something at Alice Springs at one stage, but never with the commitment that this place has had or with the beauty of this place, to be frank.

"Every hole has a dramatically different look, whereas on many golf courses, the look is very much the same."

The arid climate means Kalgoorlie Golf Course is watered with recycled effluent. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Decades of planning

After decades of lobbying, the 18-hole course opened in 2010 at a cost of $18.5 million, heavily backed by the state government and the City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder, which manages the course today.

It has faced significant challenges, serving as a lightning rod for criticism from some sections of the community for the cost burden on ratepayers.

Water shortages in a city reliant on a 560-kilometre-long pipeline for its drinking water remain an ongoing challenge, with work progressing to increase the storage capacity of dams at the golf course.

A permanent clubhouse and resort has been promised by multiple developers but is yet to be delivered, with the latest proposal stuck in legal disputes with millions of dollars of ratepayer funds already spent.

Efforts to boost tourism and attract travelling golfers have been stifled by a lack of available accommodation for those willing to make the journey.

A kangaroo at sunset at the Kalgoorlie Golf Course. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Marsh hopes those challenges can be overcome, like some of the unique problems he faced, including transforming the site of a former rubbish tip into the course's driving range.

"The brief was they wanted a golf course that was world-class, that would bring notoriety to the area, especially through Asia but Australia-wide," Marsh said.

"They wanted 36 holes, and that was in the design, until the original developer pulled out, and so things changed because it was all about money at that stage.

"Being involved in a project like this, which had such a rough start, they still allowed us to produce something that is world-class."

A new suburb has emerged from the bushland adjacent to the Kalgoorlie Golf Course since it opened in 2010. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Part of the deal to get the course built included handing over land belonging to Kalgoorlie-Boulder's then three existing golf clubs.

A portion of that land has been used for a new housing estate called GreenView, with about 250 residential lots developed next to the course and more than 2,000 lots planned in in the future.

A retirement village and a short-stay facility have also been built on other parcels of land freed up by old courses.

There are long-term plans for about 2,000 houses at the GreenView Estate in Kalgoorlie-Boulder's north-west. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

At the same time, the local game continues to grow, with 620 golf members and a renewed focus on developing junior players.

"The fact we weren't constricted by housing inside the golf course, only on the perimeter, it's what we call in the industry as being 'core golf' and that provides for a very serene and beautiful environment to play the game," Marsh said.

"It is very warming to my heart to see that golf has such a powerful role to play in developing the community."

PGA deal extended

This week has seen the course enjoying its time in the national spotlight again as the home of the WA PGA Championship.

A 120-strong field teed off on Thursday, hoping to join the ranks of several former WA PGA winners who have gone onto bigger things.

Among them is defending champion Austin Bautista, who is playing in South Africa this week and 2022 winner David Micheluzzi on the European Tour.

David Micheluzzi is sprayed with champagne after winning the 2022 WA PGA Championship at Kalgoorlie. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Kalgoorlie has hosted the WA PGA since 2012, and has locked in another five years until 2031, with the City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder's sponsorship worth more than $100,000 a year.

Mayor Glenn Wilson said it was money well spent, with the tournament watched by 412,000 viewers on pay television last year and estimates it injected $329,000 into the local economy.

"The benefits that we see from an event of this scale and magnitude go far beyond our city boundaries," he said.

"This course is unique. It's a credit to our staff."

Ben Eccles, Graham Marsh, Glenn Wilson and the PGA's Kim Felton at the Kalgoorlie Golf Course. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Victorian Ben Eccles, the 2023 WA PGA champion, said the red dirt of Kalgoorlie made it a unique and tough course to play.

"It's a world-class golf course, it gets the season off to such an awesome start and I don't think I'd be the only one to say that we all look forward to coming here," he said.

"It's a really special place for me in my career and I'll come back as long as it's held here."

Graham Marsh in 1975. (Supplied: State Library of WA)

And while Marsh says the course "has never looked better", he warned there were challenges on the horizon.

"I think robotics is going to change things, because staffing is a huge problem in this part of the world," he said.

"This course is coming up 17 years old and at 25 years, you're already starting to look at new irrigation systems because they don't last forever … you've got to have the capital, the drive and resolve to put money aside to keep it as a championship golf course.

"The worst thing you can do is sit back and pat yourself on the shoulders and say this is wonderful. If you're not looking 25 years in advance, you're not thinking long-term and that's what this place will need moving forward to keep its notoriety."

title: Oldest Wallaby remembers historic Eden Park win over All Blacks
text:
Don Strachan has accomplished a feat that only a handful of Wallabies still living have achieved — defeating the All Blacks at Eden Park.

In his second test match in 1955, the then-26-year-old prop started in Australia's 8–3 defeat of New Zealand at the iconic ground in Auckland.

The Wallabies have only tasted success against the All Blacks there on three other occasions, the last 40 years ago.

"We were determined to win that [1955] game," Strachan said.

" It was something that everyone on that team was proud of … A lot of them are not here anymore. "

An excerpt from a local newspaper following the game detailed the win as "one of the finest" the Wallabies had produced.

"The Australians gave a magnificent exhibition to outplay the All Blacks," the article said.

Don Strachan featured in the Wallabies 8–3 win over the All Blacks at Eden Park in 1955. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

Despite the victory, New Zealand retained the Bledisloe Cup following wins in the first and second test matches in Wellington and Dunedin.

The series loss still haunts Strachan all these years later.

He was disallowed a try in his debut game at Carisbrook on the South Island, which the All Blacks won 8–0.

"We were cheated," Strachan said.

Lucky to be alive

Hailing from Orange in the New South Wales Central West, the 97-year-old is the oldest living Australian rugby union player.

"I'm Wallaby number 413, and that means there are 412 of them who are no longer here anymore," he said.

"I wouldn't have wished for anything else. I've been lucky … I've had a great time."

Don Strachan is Wallaby number 413 after making his debut against the All Blacks in Dunedin in 1955. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

His international rugby career almost ended before it began following a motorbike crash in the Blue Mountains while returning from a game in Sydney.

"I had a terrific motor accident. A truck came over the hill on the wrong side of the road," Strachan said.

"[It] hit me head-on. Threw me almost into the front yard of the house next door."

After suffering a compound fracture to his leg, Strachan narrowly avoided having it amputated and spent several months in hospital.

"Their advice was that I would never be able to play rugby again because I could lose my leg," he said.

Returning to rugby

Back on his dad's potato farm near Orange, Strachan began building his strength to return to the footy field.

"I used to lift 1,000 bags of potatoes a day," he said.

"I had a very strong back, legs and shoulders … That stood me in good stead because I had the muscles to support everything else."

As a front rower, Strachan "loved the game" and the physicality that came with it.

Don Strachan remembers his time with the Wallabies fondly. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

"I never got pushed out of a scrum in my life … If they played fair, I played fair," he said.

"If they wanted to do something else, I'd accommodate them.

"I accommodated a few of them."

That love of rugby ultimately saw Strachan captain the Combined NSW Country side for five years, represent the NSW Waratahs and play twice for Australia.

Don Strachan captained the Combined NSW Country side for five years. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

It could have been more after being selected for a seven-month tour of the United Kingdom, Ireland, Canada and the United States in 1955, but with a baby on the way with wife Wendy and a farm to help run, he declined the opportunity.

Orange Emus founded

In 1947, the Orange Rugby Club had been travelling to Sydney most winter weekends to take on lifesaving clubs and agricultural schools.

From that team spawned the idea to create a four-team local competition in Orange that would become the Central West Rugby Union tournament in 1956.

The Orange Emus have won 17 first-grade premierships in the Central West Rugby Union competition, winning the Blowes Cup in 2025. (Supplied: Orange Emus)

Given that macropods had been adopted by many clubs across the country, Strachan and his friends turned to the other side of the Australian coat of arms for inspiration. And thus, the Orange Emus Rugby Club was born.

"We had a collection of some of the nicest people you could ever meet," he said.

To fund the construction of an oval and grandstand, the club had to get creative.

"We used to do these rabbit drives," Strachan said.

"We were catching 1,200 rabbits at a time and taking them into the abattoirs and selling them.

"The whole club got together and worked and made this money … eventually we were able to put it together."

The Orange Emus became one of the most successful clubs in the Central West Rugby Union competition, winning 17 first-grade titles.

The Wallabies will play NZ on Saturday afternoon.

title: 'FishTok' trend creates fishing boom among young Victorians
text:
If they were not standing on Geelong's Cunningham Pier, Ivy Renouf, Zane Winterton and Xavier Clair say they would either be hanging out in the shopping centre, playing video games, or scrolling their phones.

Instead, this trio of 16-year-olds are enjoying a day in the sun, as they try to catch some fish.

Ivy Renouf, Xavier Clair and Zane Winterton are a new breed of anglers in Geelong. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

"It's just a nice day," Ivy says.

"I didn't want to be in bed at home, or in town because I do that all the time, so I just wanted to get outdoors with my mates."

These Geelong teens are part of a new generation of Victorians getting hooked on fishing, sparking a surge of interest in the recreational activity.

Zane remembers when he was the only kid he knew who was into fishing, regularly heading out on trips with his dad.

The teenagers use an old tackle box, bait and fishing knives. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Now, he has plenty of mates who want to come along.

"When I was in primary school, before COVID, no-one fished," he says.

"It was just me, like, in the whole school.

" [Now] it's everywhere. People just fishing, putting it on their Instagram … they think they're pretty cool. "

All three of these teens say more young Victorians have been taking up fishing in the past few years, lured by both the challenge and the urge to get outside with friends.

"It's a good way to get some good memories with your friends, to be honest," Xavier says.

"Getting outside and maybe catching a fish or maybe not but, like, just hanging out with your friends and having a good time."

The trio catch little more than a pufferfish from the pier, before heading to a new spot.

At the foot of the pier they pass a group of six other young teens, who cheer each other along as they reel in a bream.

Teens carrying fishing gear through towns like Geelong has become a common sight. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

'It's been incredible'

It is hard to put a number on the increasing popularity of fishing with younger Victorians.

Victorians under 18 years old do not need a licence, and the handful of fishing clubs the ABC spoke to say they may have seen slightly more younger members signing up, but have few useful statistics to back up a boom.

Instead, they say it is an increase most visible on Victorian waterways.

Teens and young anglers throughout the state are often seen walking around clutching rods or setting up at popular fishing spots.

Anthony McGrath says it is impossible to miss the jump in fishing's popularity with young Victorians. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Anthony McGrath, executive officer at VRFish, the state's peak body for recreational fishing, says the increase in younger Victorians fishing is irrefutable.

"It's been incredible," Mr McGrath says.

"There's definitely been a massive increase in kids fishing."

"We see it here every day. The buses arrive back from schools, and the kids are walking past in school uniforms with fishing rods in hand or sticking out of their bags.

" It's something that you see now wherever you go … it's great. "

On the other side of the bay, Jet Reef Worsteling has spent much of his 19 years fishing.

He is the son of one of Australia's most famous anglers, Paul Worsteling, and is a big name on social media, counting 2.3 million followers on TikTok alone.

Jet Reef Worsteling is already a big name in fishing, particularly on social media. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"When I was in primary school and then going into high school, fishing was more of, like, was an older person's activity … it just wasn't cool like surfing or skating or any of that," Mr Worsteling says.

"I could never have pictured it in a million years, but I think the last year and a half, two years, fishing is now one of the cool things for young people to go do when they've got free time."

What's behind fishing's increasing popularity?

Those in the fishing industry point to a handful of factors behind the activity's increasing popularity with young Victorians: social media, a post-COVID desire to get outdoors, and a program handing out free fishing rods to 180,000 Victorian kids.

Mr Worsteling says there has been a clear increase in younger users getting active on "FishTok" and other platforms.

"There's definitely a lot more kids posting videos, liking videos, reacting with videos, all that sort of stuff," he says.

"I see it on my Instagram when I post a picture of a fish, or put something up, and you'll see the likes coming through, and you can just see it's young fellas, young fellas, young fellas — little grommets as we used to call them."

Mr McGrath agrees the social media boom has coincided with a post-COVID urge for people to get back outside.

"I think there's something in it with these kids, that they were the ones who were locked up when they should have been out playing," he says.

"So now we see them getting out and really engaging in these environmental type activities."

Mr McGrath says the final reason behind fishing's increasing popularity is slightly more controversial.

Victoria's Little Anglers Kits program was announced prior to the 2022 state election and handed out free fishing rods, reels, tackle boxes and information kits to about 180,000 grade 5 students across the state over the past two years.

Former premier Dan Andrews made a series of fishing announcements in the lead-up to the 2022 election. (AAP: James Ross)

But, the state government in August announced it would scrap the program, as it moves to reel in budget savings.

"We know many Victorian kids have enjoyed this program. I love fishing and we encourage Victorians to get outdoors in a range of ways," Treasurer Colin Brooks said at the time.

"Right now, we want to ensure that taxpayer dollars are wisely spent on the things that matter most."

Mr McGrath says axing the program, funded via fishing licence fees, is "cutting into the core of that access for kids to fishing".

"[The program] is us investing in our future, so we're really disappointed that the premier didn't speak to us before cutting the program, because we think it's got some long-reaching negative impacts that are yet to be seen," he says.

The government declined to respond when asked whether the Little Anglers program was considered a success.

title: Verstappen pips Russell to sprint pole at Singapore F1 grand prix
text:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen will take pole position for the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race ​on Friday, having pipped Mercedes driver George Russell, who will join him on the front row at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

Verstappen, who had never previously taken pole or won a race in Singapore, set the fastest time of one minute 31.156 seconds, 0.120 seconds quicker than Russell.

Australia's Oscar Piastri qualified fourth-fastest, just ahead of McLaren teammate Lando Norris.

"It's closer in Singapore. Your lap itself, you're pushing as hard as you think is possible, close ​to the walls in places," Verstappen said.

"Once we ‌bolted on the soft tyres, it felt like the car was coming alive a little bit more. But I did not expect this, so, of course, very happy to be first.

"The last few races we've been a lot stronger, but of course this track still highlights a few little weaknesses in the car. But we ‌managed to drive with them as well as possible."

Verstappen was investigated by the stewards for overtaking Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton under the yellow flags in SQ1. ⁠However, they accepted the Dutchman's explanation that braking could have created an unsafe situation and he had reduced his speed by lifting off the throttle afterwards.

Ferrari's ​Charles Leclerc was third fastest, while Mercedes ‌championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who leads Russell by 84 points, was only seventh quickest.

Piastri hoping for better in Singapore Oscar Piastri is hoping McLaren will be more competitive during the Singapore Grand Prix weekend after a disappointing round last time in Malaysia.

Russell was the fastest in the only practice session earlier on Friday, but his power unit penalty will not affect his position on the grid for Saturday's sprint.

However, the FIA handed the Briton a 40-place grid penalty for Sunday after he incurred a 10-place penalty for each of four additional elements, effectively consigning him to the back of ​the ‌pack.

"We've been competitive all day, from the first laps in FP1. We obviously topped the time sheets there," Russell said.

"We knew Max was fast and he went on a slightly different strategy from us in Q3, just doing the one lap. Who knows what was best, but pretty ⁠satisfied with the P2.

"It's going to be very challenging. The grip left to ‌right here is a big difference. The drivers ‌on the pole side last year had a big advantage, so it's probably going to be trying to maintain P2."

Sergio Perez brought an end to the first sprint qualifying session when he hit a barrier. (Getty Images: Clive Rose)

The first sprint qualifying session was ‌red flagged when Cadillac's Sergio Perez crashed into a barrier and attempted to nurse his car back into the pits, leaving behind debris from his front wing that marshals needed to remove.

That effectively gave drivers one lap to ‌advance to SQ2, ​and Verstappen was one of the ⁠last drivers to set a lap time, with the Dutchman topping the time sheets.

A glitch in the systems delayed the start of SQ2, with the FIA saying some lap times had not been registered. But the FIA added that the issue had been resolved and the "current timings are considered correct".

Moreover, "overtake mode" was not available after the red flag period during SQ1. It was then activated for a period ⁠of 27 seconds before being deactivated again.

"The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position ‌around the lap," it said.

"The ‌second and third periods of Sprint Qualifying were not affected."

A software bug also caused chaos last weekend. Cars slowed to a crawl on two formation laps that were held after heavy rain at Sepang forced the original start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to be aborted.

title: Cult of the Lamb video game team honours work of original composer
text:
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

Narayana Johnson had never made a game before Cult of the Lamb, one of Australia's most successful games developed by Melbourne based studio Massive Monster.

The game, equal parts cute and dark, tasks players with growing their cult of woodland followers, defeating horrifying bosses and creating a base for their flock to live.

Johnson, also known as his stage name River Boy, was the visionary behind the game's music and the sound effects.

Cult of the Lamb is one of the most popular titles produced in Australia, selling more than 7 million copies as of April this year, and its cultural impact has spread globally through fan art, cosplay and artistic performances.

The team was gearing up for the next expansion, Woolhaven, which would extend the story for the millions of players invested in the game.

Then Narayana Johnson died.

Narayana Johnson was the award-winning composer of the Cult of the Lamb soundtrack. (Supplied: Massive Monster)

Massive Monster producer Kelsey Gamble says it was a devastating time for the small team, who had to navigate the loss of one of their beloved coworkers while continuing to make a game of which he was an integral part.

"How could you possibly fathom something like this happening and then just move on?" she tells ABC News.

"The answer was, we couldn't. We stopped, you know, everybody obviously took time off to process."

Taking time to grieve

The studio stopped work on the expansion, instead prototyping small games, before returning to development proper.

The first step was to pick up the pieces already completed, with some tracks and the overall 'sonic identity' of Woolhaven already established.

That included finding Johnson's laptop, and then unlocking it to get the raw files already finished.

Cult of the Lamb blended the chilled-out base-building of the Animal Crossing series with satanic cults and ritual sacrifice, to great success. (ABC News)

Johnson had been working with singer and songwriter Ray Vavasis, who performs as Arrowbird, on a couple of tracks for the expansion at the time of his passing.

Johnson's niece, and one half of his band Willow Beats, Kalyani Ellis also wrote music for the game.

JoJo Zhou, head of narrative at Massive Monster, says Vavasis's existing attachment to the project made a huge difference.

"Ray was an absolute godsend the way that she was able to continue the work that Narayana had started, even though often the rest of us were kind of scrambling about what we were going to do," she says.

" Ray would make something and it would give you this feeling that Narayana would have loved this and that was just such a good metric. "

One small snippet composed collaboratively

Vavasis says while working on a teaser trailer for the game, she and Johnson developed a short snippet of music with vocals that was originally planned to be expanded to a full track.

While that never happened, it did become the foundation of much of the work after.

"When writing for the game I would use bits we hadn't finished yet, to pay homage," she says.

"Naturally that's what I wanted to do but it was also a way to process grief.

"That little snippet I ended up using in a lot of things, lots of different scenes."

"I was committed to this project but I felt like upholding that legacy gave me the strength of two people."

Cult of the Lamb composer Ray Vavasis, aka Arrowbird, and head of narrative JoJo Zhou speaking at High Score 2026 at ACMI in Melbourne. (ABC Arts: Gianfranco Di Giovanni)

At the 2026 High Score conference this week, Massive Monster announced the memorial River Boy Scholarship to support composers to make music for games.

Funding, mentorship, access to co-working desks and studio space would be offered to successful participants Zhou says.

"The River Boy Scholarship is about helping composers make the leap from their discipline, into games," she says.

" Narayana didn't come from a games background; Ray doesn't, I don't, and it's incredibly important that we support that diversity of perspective in his memory. "

The River Boy Scholarship will open for applications in 2027.

title: Tasmanian EPA says it was not told extent of Firmus data centre generator plans
text:
Tasmania's environmental regulator is urging a tribunal to hear its concerns, after learning the operator of a recently approved AI data centre wants to use hundreds of diesel generators far more often than it originally disclosed.

Earlier this year, the George Town Council approved a Firmus Technologies proposal to build a 288-megawatt data centre in the state's north, after the Tasmanian Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) determined it did not need to make an environmental assessment.

The data centre's approval was subject to conditions, including that Firmus could only run the 276 on-site diesel generators at limited times, such as during emergencies or routine inspections.

Firmus Technologies is building AI data centres in Tasmania, but most of its planned centres are not built yet. (Supplied: Firmus Technologies)

Firmus, however, has appealed that condition through the Tasmanian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (TASCAT), arguing it wanted to use the generators "for limited augmentation of the mains electricity supply to offset curtailment, manage energy security and maintain operational reliability during periods of energy market stress".

Tasmania's Environment Protection Authority (EPA) board has now applied to TASCAT to join as a party to Firmus's appeal.

EPA likely to have assessed project if proposed use was higher

In its October 7 submission, seen by the ABC, the board said it was originally told the generators would be used "just for emergency use in the event of a power failure", and would not be used during normal operation other than for scheduled weekly exercise runs of less than two hours, annual load tests, and utility outage events.

The board said Firmus's recent appeal showed it planned on using the generators in more circumstances than it thought.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff (centre) with co-CEOs Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis at the Firmus Technologies site. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

"That variation, if part of the original proposal, would likely have resulted in the Board making a different decision in relation to whether to assess the proposal," the board said.

" Seeking to enlarge the use of the diesel generators post-approval undermines the Board's determination and changes the environmental risk profile posed by the activity. "

It pointed out that if Firmus's appeal against the condition around generator use is upheld, it could allow it to subvert EPA processes it likely would have been subjected to "if the proposal had been accurately presented".

"And further, if upheld, the appeal has the potential to permit an activity in circumstances where the environmental risks have not been properly assessed, which may result in environmental harm including nuisance … necessitating the EPA taking enforcement action in respect of it," it said.

Construction underway at Firmus's St Leonards site. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The EPA board said it would not comment on matters currently being considered by TASCAT, and Firmus declined to comment on the matter.

A state government spokesperson said it was supportive of private investments that created jobs and economic benefits but "projects should use resources responsibly and engage transparently with communities".

Greens MP Tabatha Badger said she welcomed the EPA raising concerns and pointing out the potential for the generators to breach acceptable limits and for noise to carry across the river.

"Victoria is already moving towards rules for AI data centres that ensure diesel generators are only used only as a back-up. That's the kind of standard that should be applied in Tasmania too," she said

Backflip on energy generation

Meanwhile, a submission made by Firmus to the current federal joint select committee on AI reveals its Tasmanian data centres may be powered with renewable infrastructure based interstate, rather than locally.

Firmus has long said it will build two megawatts of new renewable energy generation for every 1 megawatt it uses across new data centres planned for Launceston, Long Reach and Wesley Vale.

Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis are the co-CEOs of Firmus Technologies. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Firmus's co-CEO Tim Rosenfield has previously implied that new capacity would be built in Tasmania.

"[Firmus investment] will add net new energy to Tasmania that will end up being able to be exported across Marinus [Link], which is a good thing we feel," he told ABC Mornings in July.

But according to Firmus's recent submission, which it engaged Oxford Economics Australia to prepare, those renewable projects are "not necessarily sited within Tasmania".

"Those commitments are defined at the level of Firmus' contracting rather than by location, so the capacity underwritten is delivered into the National Electricity Market as a whole and is not necessarily sited within Tasmania," it said.

Firmus declined to comment.

The company is currently negotiating with Hydro Tasmania to secure 444MW of power for its centres.

A Hydro Tasmania spokesperson said the new renewable projects it was considering as part of its assessment of Firmus's request "are all located in Tasmania, in line with the Tasmanian government's expectations that data centres in Tasmania support new on-island energy generation".

A Tasmanian government spokesperson said it expected developers to unlock new renewable energy generation projects in Tasmania to support their demand.

title: Darwin council leads China and Vietnam delegation after rate rise
text:
Darwin City Council has defended its decision to lead a trade delegation to Asia during a year when the city's rates have been hiked and its annual hard rubbish collection delayed to 2027.

The council has confirmed about $18,000 of ratepayer funding will be spent on the mission, to be led by lord mayor Peter Styles, which aims to open economic doors for the Top End city.

The council's general manager of innovation, Alice Percy, said the delegation would lead about 10 businesses to Guangzhou in China and Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam in December.

Guangzhou, China's third-largest city, will be part of the council-led trade delegation. (Getty Images)

"This is definitely not a junket for the mayor and for the council," she said.

"It's an important economic opportunity for Darwin as a capital city."

Ms Percy said it would be the first time the city's council had led a delegation abroad since 2023.

"The economic impact of these types of trade missions can lead to approximately $250,000 per annum coming into the economy," she said.

Alice Percy says the trade mission could be lucrative for the Darwin economy. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

The delegation comes a year after China Southern Airlines began flying to and from Darwin, with the council voicing its ambition to try and convince more carriers to fly to the city.

While attending businesses will fund their own trips, the council has said it will provide support and facilitate introductions and networking opportunities with businesses in Asia.

Mr Styles is a previous NT government Asian engagement minister, and after he lost his seat in 2016, he held private consultancy businesses in the same field.

Peter Styles will lead the delegation. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

The council was asked whether it viewed Mr Styles's previous roles as possible conflicts of interest in leading the delegation, but it did not respond by deadline.

Mr Styles was unavailable for an interview.

Trip follows rate rises, service delay

The council's move to embark on the trip comes six months after it raised rates by 5.5 per cent, above inflation level, and ditched its annual pre-cyclone clean-up for 2026, postponing it until next May.

At the time of the rate hike, Mr Styles said the council was grappling with rising expenses and a large damage bill following a destructive cyclone season.

The trip will also take in Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City. (ABC News: Jarrod Fankhauser)

Former Darwin lord mayor Graeme Sawyer said the council risked seeming out of touch with its ratepayers.

"Particularly at a time when cost of living and everything else is so front and centre in people's minds, you're really treading on some rough country here," he said.

Mr Sawyer said he had concerns about a "culture of secrecy" within the Darwin council, where discussed items were routinely being made confidential and unable to be viewed by the public.

Graeme Sawyer says the council should be "open and explicit" with ratepayers about its reasons for ventures like this one. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"If council's not being open and explicit about the benefits and the reasons for these sorts of things, then naturally people are just going to think it's another junket," he said.

The Asian trade delegation was originally made confidential by the council when the resolution was passed earlier this year, but the council has confirmed it has now been made public.

In the community, the ABC asked Darwin residents what they thought of the upcoming trade mission, which will fund two council staff members to travel abroad alongside the lord mayor.

Kathy Carter would like to see the council focus more on rates, roads and rubbish. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Darwin resident of more than 40 years, Kathy Carter, said she did not support the initiative.

"I think it's probably not a good idea," she said.

"The rates have just been put up, and we need more interest in rates, roads and rubbish.

"They can do cultural ties and trading things and all that stuff with the [NT] government."

Mike Sproule says the money going towards the delegation could be better spent elsewhere. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Resident of The Gardens for more than 30 years, Mike Sproule, said he had "found over the last couple of years the performance of the council seems to be struggling".

"I'm all for cultural ties and growing business, but … it just seems to be a bit of a waste of money, really," he said.

Darwin City Council has said the trade mission will be held between December 8 and 16.

He flagged one of the hardest problems ahead: “I think people do and will feel that they’re training technology.”

Advertisement

‘Barcodes with a pulse’ For many of the country’s lowest-paid workers, AI already acts as the boss, according to their union. The Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association represents 200,000 retail, fast food and warehouse workers. Its chief of staff, Robert Tonkli, told the committee on Wednesday that AI already sets their rosters, hands out their tasks and increasingly decides who gets performance managed. The union’s submission tells of a supermarket worker with more than 30 years’ service who received a final written warning for scanning errors. An AI checkout system, using overhead cameras to match items against scans, generated it. She got about one item wrong in every 533, an error rate of roughly 0.18 per cent. Nobody ever told her what error rate the system would accept. The union has challenged the warning. Labor senator Tony Sheldon. Dominic Lorrimer At Aldi’s NSW distribution centres, the submission says, new picking benchmarks generated from warehouse data arrived without consultation with workers or the union. Aldi management reported throughput up 16 per cent and labour costs down 26 per cent. Workers surveyed by the union reported strain, exhaustion and injuries, and said missing the targets could cost them a warning or their job.

Advertisement

“Aldi rejects claims that the Picking Efficiency benchmarking puts employee safety at risk,” an Aldi spokesperson said. “Aldi consults with our people and provides training to support the rollout of any new process.” The spokesman said Aldi recently met the union and invited it to provide specific details of its concerns so they could be investigated, and has not yet received them. Sheldon said the union’s examples amounted to “treating people like barcodes with a pulse”. Employers push back hard on this: The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry told the committee in its submission there was “insufficient evidence demonstrating systemic workplace harms arising from AI”. Existing work health and safety, unfair dismissal and consultation laws already apply, it said. The last great shutdown Australia has been through mass job losses before. Ford shut its Geelong plant in October 2016. Toyota at Altona and Holden at Elizabeth followed a year later. A 2019 evaluation for the federal employment department credited the carmakers’ long notice for much of what went right. It counted about $380 million in support from the federal, Victorian and South Australian governments and the carmakers, which also covered supply chain workers and programs for parts suppliers. Ford ended its Australian car production in 2016. Penny Stephens

Advertisement

About 14,000 jobs went in the end – about $27,000 for each one. Victoria’s $14 million AI package aims to help more than 6200 workers retrain, about $2260 each. The federal government’s National AI Plan sets aside no equivalent fund for workers displaced by AI. CBA’s $90 million program works out at about $1700 a head over three years, spread across about 51,700 full-time staff. The bank’s money goes to every employee, not only those whose jobs are at risk. Anthropic’s head of product policy, Charlie Hale, and head of policy, David Masters, at the federal parliamentary AI inquiry at State Parliament House. Wolter Peeters Even with that money, the car workers’ recovery was uneven. Andrew Beer, executive dean of the University of South Australia’s business school, tracked them from 2020 to 2024. By the end, about 72 per cent had work and fewer than 4 per cent were unemployed. But a partner’s wage and the family home carried them further than the labour market did, and the youngest fared worst.

Advertisement

“What happens to the 45-year-old woman working in accounts receivable who is made redundant as AI takes her role?” Beer asked. Workers like her, he told this masthead, “move down the workforce hierarchy – lower pay, less buoyant industry – aiming to make do, rather than get ahead.” ‘Very good at nodding’ None of this changes unless parliament acts. In November 2024, the Senate committee on adopting AI that Sheldon chaired made 13 recommendations, including extending workplace safety protections to cover AI. On Tuesday, Sheldon was still pushing for workplace safety law to cover AI. This committee has at least dragged some commitments onto the record. Anthropic said whether it tells governments about incidents is “probably controlled by Anthropic internal policy right now”, and both it and OpenAI said they would back laws forcing disclosure. Assistant minister Andrew Charlton said on Thursday the Medicare incident would shape the national AI standards the government has promised to legislate. The voice actors have been lobbying Canberra for years. Politicians, Kennedy told the committee, are “very good at nodding”. “I don’t mean that in a cynical way. I mean that they hear what we say and they’re like, ‘That makes plenty of sense’.” Then he added: “Of course, then action is required.”

Advertisement

Duncan’s first ask: tell audiences when a performer is not real. “If someone wants to present a human that is AI-generated in any way, the audience should know,” she said. The committee reports on November 30. Its options run from mandatory reporting of AI incidents to a levy on AI companies to pay creators, which the alliance wants. The retail union is pushing for an expert AI panel inside the Fair Work Commission. None of it binds the government, which has so far preferred existing laws to new ones. Kwon left parliament in a tinted van, giving muted answers about how the Medicare breach had happened. Duncan still reads commercials when the bookings come, but she has no way of tracking what happens to the recording. “Consent should never be assumed,” she said. A two-bedroom corner Victorian terrace in Kensington owned by North Melbourne defender Luke McDonald sold to first home buyers for $1.06 million at auction on Saturday. Held by the Kangaroos player since 2018, 1 Albermarle Street has been updated throughout – with polished floorboards, a stepped open living and dining room, new kitchen and bathroom, and a landscaped garden – while maintaining its classic front. The property was listed with a price guide of $900,000 to $990,000 on the last weekend before new legislation kicks in requiring vendors to advertise their reserve at least seven days before an auction. The new laws come into effect on October 16. Nelson Alexander Flemington agent and auctioneer Ryan Currie said he had “pre-empted the new legislation” and told buyers during the week, as well as in his auction preamble, that the reserve in Kensington was $990,000.

Advertisement

Currie opened the auction with a vendor bid of $900,000, which was matched by a genuine bid. Another vendor bid took it to $920,000, followed by a genuine bid of $940,000. Related Article Property market Kangaroos defender Luke McDonald lists Kensington home for $900,000-$990,000 From the moment it hit $940,000, Currie said, increments of $10,000 and $20,000 from the two bidders pushed it to $990,000 in less than 10 seconds. The auctioneer declared the home on the market, and said the rest of the bids were so quick that “the whole auction was done in less than 40 seconds”. “The vendor was sunning himself [on holiday],” he said, and McDonald’s sister attended the auction while on the phone to him.

McDonald and wife Brooklyn initially lived in the home and kept it as an investment. It was the first purchase for the buyers, a couple renting nearby, Currie said. The property was one of 698 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. The home has been updated to make the most of its layout. Nelson Alexander Flemington In Armadale, a three-bedroom Edwardian home sold for $1.75 million at auction, with four bidders rocketing it more than $300,000 above its $1.44 million reserve. Moments from both Glenferrie Road and High Street, 5 Stanhope Street features terracotta tiled floors, open-plan living and a bricked rear terrace with right-of-way access, and had a price guide of $1.35 million to $1.45 million.

After the property was declared on the market, another two bidders joined the fray, and a mix of $10,000 and $5000 increments sent the home soaring $400,000 past the opening bid to sell to a young professional. Fetter said bidders were a mix of couples and singles. The home was sold as a deceased estate. She said the upcoming reserve disclosure requirement was a “massive change”, and expected some trial and error from buyers, sellers and agents as they “try to navigate” it.

A young couple from Homebush bought their first house on Saturday, paying $2.55 million for a three-bedroom Five Dock property, $100,000 above the reserve. About 20 people gathered in the open-plan kitchen and living area to the rear of 9 Ingham Avenue on a wet morning as all four registered bidders raised their paddles, vying for the keys to the single-fronted, single-level home. Bidding opened at $2.3 million, $100,000 below the $2.4 million guide. After the first increment of $50,000, bids fell back to smaller amounts of $25,000, $20,000 and $10,000, with auctioneer Ricky Briggs from Apollo Auctions fielding offers, at times in rapid-fire succession. After just six minutes and more than 20 bids, a final bid of $5000 sealed the deal and the hammer fell, with the property selling to the young couple, who were upgrading from an apartment.

Advertisement

Related Article Auctions Inner west art deco apartment sells for $900k to Bondi couple It had a reserve of $2.45 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. The underbidders were a couple living in Coogee who had been priced out of their local market. One member of the couple had grown up in the Five Dock region and saw value in the area. The property is a deceased estate.

Advertisement

The living area leads onto a deck with extendable awning. Domain Briggs said the quick result was evidence that “A-grade products” always performed well, although he said the latest interest rate increase had affected buyer sentiment. “As a whole, consumer confidence is down, with numbers at auctions and registered bidders dipping slightly,” he said. “Attendance numbers have significantly reduced as well.” Auctioneer Ricky Briggs kept pace with bidders, taking more than 20 bids in six minutes. James Brickwood Antonio Ariola, sales agent for Belle Property Drummoyne, said the “neat and tidy” property came with desirable amenities, including two bathrooms, two living areas and a small studio or storage shed at the rear. The home is also positioned within walking distance of the popular Five Dock and Haberfield cafe and shopping precincts, known for their Italian influence, and has easy access to local schools and public transport.

Advertisement

“For the right property and right location, there is definitely a market, but it is down to vendors listening to buyers,” Ariola said. The property was one of 637 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. In Marrickville a young couple renting locally won the keys to their first home on Saturday, paying $981,000 for a two-bedroom apartment. Three parties registered to bid for the first-floor, mid-century home at 2/35-37 Pile Street, with two active. Bidding opened quickly at $950,000, the same as the guide, going up in increments of $5000 and $1000 until it reached $976,000, when it stalled.

Advertisement

One party made a further bid of $4000 to $980,000, at which point the reserve was renegotiated to $1 million. The same bidder then increased their bid to $981,000 and the property sold. The successful bidders were attracted to the boutique size of the block, which has 10 units, and the quiet, tree-lined street. The underbidder was an owner-occupier seeking to return to the Marrickville area from north-west Sydney. The vendor is hoping to upsize. The two-bedroom apartment is in a boutique block of just 10. Domain Norman Tran, sales agent for Adrian William, said the size of the bids and readjusted reserve were an indication that there was still a “price sensitivity” in the market. “That is requiring vendors to realign expectations if they want to sell,” he said.

Advertisement

Turnkey properties are also giving vendors the edge, he said, as buyers shy away from the added expense of renovating. “Properties which are well presented and updated are proving to be more popular,” he said. “Buyers are not as interested in renovating.” Related Article Renting ‘Losing hope’: Why renting in Sydney is getting so much harder – for everyone In Sutherland a young couple expecting their first child successfully bid for a five-bedroom home with pool, paying $1.88 million. Four parties registered to bid for 24a Glencoe Street, including groups on the phone from France and Britain, with three active.

Bidding opened at $1.7 million, the same as the guide, followed by increments of $50,000, and then $10,000, $5000 and $1000 before the hammer fell. The property had a reserve of $1.8 million. The winning bidders and the underbidder, an English-Australian couple who had first seen the property when they were overseas, were both on site. The vendor plans to downsize. The single-level home sits on a 790.8-square-metre block and is designed for open-plan living. Domain Luke Lombardi, sales agent for Pulse Property Agents, described the auction as “quick and effective”. He said the latest interest rate rise had motivated some buyers to act.

“Buyers are cautious that if another rate rise happens, their preapproval [loan] finishes, and they may lose some of their budget.”

Here are the top marquee men – if they don’t come to terms with their incumbent clubs beforehand – that will be testing their market value. Nathan Cleary (Penrith Panthers) This is the biggest domino to fall in the transfer market. Undoubtedly the best and most influential player in the NRL, which will make Cleary’s the most sought-after signature in the game. The horrific leg injury suffered in the preliminary final is a curveball that nobody saw coming, but that won’t deter Penrith or other clubs from trying to secure his services.
