title: Why the Russian plague lab case is unlikely to cause the next pandemic
text:
IN BRIEF The cause of Darya Shipilova's fatal pneumonia remains unknown as Russia denies risk of further outbreak.

Experts say an plague outbreak in Australia is 'extremely unlikely', but more information is crucial.

Limited facts and circulating misinformation have fuelled international panic about the death of a Russian lab worker from an unidentified source of pneumonia. But Australian experts say there's no threat of a global health crisis.

Darya Shipilova, an employee at the Russian Anti-Plague Research Institute in Irkutsk, southern Siberia, died in early October after contracting pneumonia, Russian health authorities have said.

Despite introducing sweeping preventative health measures, they have since said that there is no further risk to the population.

However, limited information has been released about the cause of the 28-year-old's pneumonia, and the World Health Organization (WHO) is seeking further answers from Russia.

The Australian Centre for Disease Control (CDC) told SBS News there is "no evidence to suggest an increased risk to the Australian public from this event at this time".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The organisation said that while it's aware of the death, "verified information remains limited".

"The Australian CDC is engaged through established international public health networks and is monitoring the situation closely," it said. "We will continue to assess the situation as further information becomes available."

Associate Professor Suman Majumdar, chief health officer at Melbourne's Burnet Institute, a leading scientific research centre, told SBS News there is "no reason for Australians to be alarmed".

"At this stage, we have a serious and unusual death with unanswered questions, but we do not have evidence of a plague outbreak, or a risk to Australia," he said.

Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, confirmed Shipilova's death on 2 October, two days after she became ill.

READ MORE The telltale sign Russia's plague scare could be more serious

It confirmed she was vaccinated and was "immune to the dangerous infections with which she worked".

Pneumonia is a lung infection that can be caused by a variety of conditions, including plague, flu, or COVID-19. There has been no information released clarifying what caused Shipilova's pneumonia or how she contracted the illness.

Rospotrebnadzor said there is no danger of an outbreak, with almost 200 people quarantined in preventative measures.

"As of October 7, 2026, medical monitoring has been completed for over 90 per cent of contacts," the agency said.

"No health issues related to infectious diseases were detected, and the result of nearly 5,000 laboratory tests revealed no dangerous pathogenic microorganisms."

Infectious disease expert and clinical microbiologist, Professor Paul Griffin said it's "concerning" that Shipilova worked in a laboratory with the Yersinia pestis bacteria, which causes the plague. The same bacteria was responsible for the Black Death that killed tens of millions of people in Europe between 1346 and 1353.

"There's no confirmation that is related to her work, but we also haven't heard or seen the actual results of the testing to verify that — or the results to say what she actually passed away from," he said.

"We certainly do need more information, but at this stage it doesn't seem like this is something that's not going to be able to be readily contained."

'Transparent information sharing' crucial to global safety

This lack of information has concerned the WHO, which initially deemed the death to be a low risk to global public health.

However, it has since changed its messaging.

"We don't yet have the full picture of this event and we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment," said WHO director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.

"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential risks".

WHO department of epidemic and pandemic management director, Maria Van Kerkhove said the organisation wants "more information to understand which laboratory tests were conducted, which pathogens were evaluated".

She said if Russia confirmed Shipilova did not die from the plague, the cause of the fatal pneumonia should be determined and that information shared.

Kerkhove said the WHO had contacted Russia's health ministry requesting "further answers".

Russia denies it has not fully informed the WHO about the death, saying it has provided information "in accordance with established practice".

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov claimed the media was responsible for circulating misinformation and causing concern.

Griffin said the lack of information sharing may result from "perception issues and other potential sensitivities geopolitically".

"It's difficult to know what the motives would be for not providing the information required."

The microbiologist said "transparent, real-time, open disclosure" is needed to "allay everyone's concerns".

'No evidence' of another pandemic

Majumdar from the Burnet Institute said that the "lack of information" about the cause of Shipilova's pneumonia is "not evidence that a larger outbreak is occurring".

While Shipilova worked in an anti-plague laboratory, both Griffin and Majumdar said there's no chance that an outbreak of the plague would be as serious or severe as the COVID-19 pandemic.

"There are literally no parallels that are reasonable to COVID-19," Griffin said.

He said that typically seven people die in the United States annually from the plague.

"It's not something that's gone away ... this organism has been around for many hundreds, if not thousands of years. We know a lot about it. It's nowhere near as easily transmissible as COVID."

READ MORE What we know about the mysterious death at a Russian plague institute

Majumdar said the bacterial infection can be easily treated.

"We have diagnostic tests and treatments. Antibiotics are effective, particularly when treatment begins early, and people who have been exposed can also be given antibiotics before they develop symptoms," he said.

"Unlike COVID-19 or influenza, the plague is not known for widespread sustained community transmission from people with mild or no symptoms."

According to Griffin, Australia's health system and laboratory safety standards are "so robust" that an outbreak or incident is "so extremely unlikely".

"If it were to happen, our systems would kick in so swiftly to ensure the safety of everyone involved, including potential contacts," he said.

"We would be on the front foot by communicating this to relevant authorities and the public to make sure there was no undue alarm."

Last financial year, Duncan earned about 30 per cent of what she had consistently made in the three years before. She now works a second job. “AI voices and performances have definitely played a big part,” she told this masthead. Clients have also used them to push down the rates the union spent years fighting for, she said. “It’s faster and cheaper, so therefore we should be as well.” Duncan, the NSW president of Equity, the performers’ division of the media union, gave evidence to the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence. “I never gave consent for my work to be taken,” she said. “Our members are already 62 per cent down on their work in the last 12 months,” Simon Kennedy, president of the Australian Association of Voice Actors, told the same hearing. Jacqui Duncan has voiced more than 5000 commercials for Australian radio and television. Over two days in Sydney and then two in Melbourne, witness after witness described AI reshaping work for voice actors, bank staff and supermarket workers.

When Ford, Toyota and Holden shut their Australian plants, workers got three years’ warning and about $380 million in support from governments and the carmakers. Victoria has put up $14 million for workers at risk from AI. ‘It’s about consent’ Related Article Opinion

AI I owe an AI panic sceptic a beer. But she was only half right David Swan Technology editor OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google all put Canberra on notice – Australia’s copyright rules will dictate whether they train their flagship models on local soil. But copyright usually belongs to a studio, label, publisher or advertiser, not to the performer or writer who made the work. Under the deals and funds on the table, the alliance warned, the money flows to whoever holds the copyright. Duncan has never held the copyright to her own commercials. “But if it’s my biometric data and 20 years of industry skills that go into those performances, I should have a say,” she said. Clients, she said, should not get a performance at all if it “only exists because mine and thousands of others’ training, performance skills, experience and creative consciousness have all been whittled down to ones and zeros, fed into an LLM (for free) and then exported”.

She knows voice artists and actors who have been replaced by AI copies of themselves, their voices or faces used in new campaigns without consent or payment. When one colleague asked a producer why he had not even been consulted, Duncan said, the producer replied that he “assumed consent was given”. “It feels violating,” she said. “It’s not about payment; it’s about consent,” Kennedy told the committee. “Opting out after the fact is too late because you cannot un-violate somebody.”

The Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association represents 200,000 retail, fast food and warehouse workers. Its chief of staff, Robert Tonkli, told the committee on Wednesday that AI already sets their rosters, hands out their tasks and increasingly decides who gets performance managed. The union’s submission tells of a supermarket worker with more than 30 years’ service who received a final written warning for scanning errors. Nobody ever told her what error rate the system would accept. The union has challenged the warning. Labor senator Tony Sheldon. Sheldon said the union’s examples amounted to “treating people like barcodes with a pulse”. Employers push back hard on this: The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry told the committee in its submission there was “insufficient evidence demonstrating systemic workplace harms arising from AI”. Existing work health and safety, unfair dismissal and consultation laws already apply, it said. The last great shutdown Australia has been through mass job losses before. Ford shut its Geelong plant in October 2016. Toyota at Altona and Holden at Elizabeth followed a year later. A 2019 evaluation for the federal employment department credited the carmakers’ long notice for much of what went right. It counted about $380 million in support from the federal, Victorian and South Australian governments and the carmakers, which also covered supply chain workers and programs for parts suppliers. Ford ended its Australian car production in 2016. Penny Stephens

Advertisement

About 14,000 jobs went in the end – about $27,000 for each one. Victoria’s $14 million AI package aims to help more than 6200 workers retrain, about $2260 each. The federal government’s National AI Plan sets aside no equivalent fund for workers displaced by AI. CBA’s $90 million program works out at about $1700 a head over three years, spread across about 51,700 full-time staff. The bank’s money goes to every employee, not only those whose jobs are at risk. Anthropic’s head of product policy, Charlie Hale, and head of policy, David Masters, at the federal parliamentary AI inquiry at State Parliament House. Wolter Peeters Even with that money, the car workers’ recovery was uneven. Andrew Beer, executive dean of the University of South Australia’s business school, tracked them from 2020 to 2024. By the end, about 72 per cent had work and fewer than 4 per cent were unemployed. But a partner’s wage and the family home carried them further than the labour market did, and the youngest fared worst.

Advertisement

“What happens to the 45-year-old woman working in accounts receivable who is made redundant as AI takes her role?” Beer asked. Workers like her, he told this masthead, “move down the workforce hierarchy – lower pay, less buoyant industry – aiming to make do, rather than get ahead.” ‘Very good at nodding’ None of this changes unless parliament acts. In November 2024, the Senate committee on adopting AI that Sheldon chaired made 13 recommendations, including extending workplace safety protections to cover AI. On Tuesday, Sheldon was still pushing for workplace safety law to cover AI. This committee has at least dragged some commitments onto the record. Anthropic said whether it tells governments about incidents is “probably controlled by Anthropic internal policy right now”, and both it and OpenAI said they would back laws forcing disclosure. Assistant minister Andrew Charlton said on Thursday the Medicare incident would shape the national AI standards the government has promised to legislate. The voice actors have been lobbying Canberra for years. Politicians, Kennedy told the committee, are “very good at nodding”. “I don’t mean that in a cynical way. I mean that they hear what we say and they’re like, ‘That makes plenty of sense’.” Then he added: “Of course, then action is required.”

Advertisement

Duncan’s first ask: tell audiences when a performer is not real. “If someone wants to present a human that is AI-generated in any way, the audience should know,” she said. The committee reports on November 30. Its options run from mandatory reporting of AI incidents to a levy on AI companies to pay creators, which the alliance wants. The retail union is pushing for an expert AI panel inside the Fair Work Commission. None of it binds the government, which has so far preferred existing laws to new ones. Kwon left parliament in a tinted van, giving muted answers about how the Medicare breach had happened. Duncan still reads commercials when the bookings come, but she has no way of tracking what happens to the recording. “Consent should never be assumed,” she said. A two-bedroom corner Victorian terrace in Kensington owned by North Melbourne defender Luke McDonald sold to first home buyers for $1.06 million at auction on Saturday. Held by the Kangaroos player since 2018, 1 Albermarle Street has been updated throughout – with polished floorboards, a stepped open living and dining room, new kitchen and bathroom, and a landscaped garden – while maintaining its classic front. The property was listed with a price guide of $900,000 to $990,000 on the last weekend before new legislation kicks in requiring vendors to advertise their reserve at least seven days before an auction. The new laws come into effect on October 16. Nelson Alexander Flemington agent and auctioneer Ryan Currie said he had “pre-empted the new legislation” and told buyers during the week, as well as in his auction preamble, that the reserve in Kensington was $990,000.

Currie opened the auction with a vendor bid of $900,000, which was matched by a genuine bid. Another vendor bid took it to $920,000, followed by a genuine bid of $940,000. Related Article Property market Kangaroos defender Luke McDonald lists Kensington home for $900,000-$990,000 From the moment it hit $940,000, Currie said, increments of $10,000 and $20,000 from the two bidders pushed it to $990,000 in less than 10 seconds. The auctioneer declared the home on the market, and said the rest of the bids were so quick that “the whole auction was done in less than 40 seconds”. “The vendor was sunning himself [on holiday],” he said, and McDonald’s sister attended the auction while on the phone to him.

McDonald and wife Brooklyn initially lived in the home and kept it as an investment. It was the first purchase for the buyers, a couple renting nearby, Currie said. The property was one of 698 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. The home has been updated to make the most of its layout. Nelson Alexander Flemington In Armadale, a three-bedroom Edwardian home sold for $1.75 million at auction, with four bidders rocketing it more than $300,000 above its $1.44 million reserve. Fetter said bidders were a mix of couples and singles. The home was sold as a deceased estate. A young couple from Homebush bought their first house on Saturday, paying $2.55 million for a three-bedroom Five Dock property, $100,000 above the reserve. About 20 people gathered in the open-plan kitchen and living area to the rear of 9 Ingham Avenue on a wet morning as all four registered bidders raised their paddles, vying for the keys to the single-fronted, single-level home. Bidding opened at $2.3 million, $100,000 below the $2.4 million guide. After the first increment of $50,000, bids fell back to smaller amounts of $25,000, $20,000 and $10,000, with auctioneer Ricky Briggs from Apollo Auctions fielding offers, at times in rapid-fire succession. After just six minutes and more than 20 bids, a final bid of $5000 sealed the deal and the hammer fell, with the property selling to the young couple, who were upgrading from an apartment.

Advertisement

Related Article Auctions Inner west art deco apartment sells for $900k to Bondi couple It had a reserve of $2.45 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. The underbidders were a couple living in Coogee who had been priced out of their local market. One member of the couple had grown up in the Five Dock region and saw value in the area. The property is a deceased estate.

Advertisement

The living area leads onto a deck with extendable awning. Domain Briggs said the quick result was evidence that “A-grade products” always performed well, although he said the latest interest rate increase had affected buyer sentiment. “As a whole, consumer confidence is down, with numbers at auctions and registered bidders dipping slightly,” he said. “Attendance numbers have significantly reduced as well.” Auctioneer Ricky Briggs kept pace with bidders, taking more than 20 bids in six minutes. James Brickwood Antonio Ariola, sales agent for Belle Property Drummoyne, said the “neat and tidy” property came with desirable amenities, including two bathrooms, two living areas and a small studio or storage shed at the rear. The home is also positioned within walking distance of the popular Five Dock and Haberfield cafe and shopping precincts, known for their Italian influence, and has easy access to local schools and public transport.

Advertisement

“For the right property and right location, there is definitely a market, but it is down to vendors listening to buyers,” Ariola said. The property was one of 637 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. In Marrickville a young couple renting locally won the keys to their first home on Saturday, paying $981,000 for a two-bedroom apartment. Three parties registered to bid for the first-floor, mid-century home at 2/35-37 Pile Street, with two active. Bidding opened quickly at $950,000, the same as the guide, going up in increments of $5000 and $1000 until it reached $976,000, when it stalled.

Advertisement

One party made a further bid of $4000 to $980,000, at which point the reserve was renegotiated to $1 million. The same bidder then increased their bid to $981,000 and the property sold. The successful bidders were attracted to the boutique size of the block, which has 10 units, and the quiet, tree-lined street. The underbidder was an owner-occupier seeking to return to the Marrickville area from north-west Sydney. The vendor is hoping to upsize. The two-bedroom apartment is in a boutique block of just 10. Domain Norman Tran, sales agent for Adrian William, said the size of the bids and readjusted reserve were an indication that there was still a “price sensitivity” in the market. “That is requiring vendors to realign expectations if they want to sell,” he said.

Advertisement

Turnkey properties are also giving vendors the edge, he said, as buyers shy away from the added expense of renovating. “Properties which are well presented and updated are proving to be more popular,” he said. “Buyers are not as interested in renovating.” Related Article Renting ‘Losing hope’: Why renting in Sydney is getting so much harder – for everyone In Sutherland a young couple expecting their first child successfully bid for a five-bedroom home with pool, paying $1.88 million. Four parties registered to bid for 24a Glencoe Street, including groups on the phone from France and Britain, with three active.

Bidding opened at $1.7 million, the same as the guide, followed by increments of $50,000, and then $10,000, $5000 and $1000 before the hammer fell. The property had a reserve of $1.8 million. The winning bidders and the underbidder, an English-Australian couple who had first seen the property when they were overseas, were both on site. The vendor plans to downsize. The single-level home sits on a 790.8-square-metre block and is designed for open-plan living. Domain Luke Lombardi, sales agent for Pulse Property Agents, described the auction as “quick and effective”. He said the latest interest rate rise had motivated some buyers to act.

“Buyers are cautious that if another rate rise happens, their preapproval [loan] finishes, and they may lose some of their budget.”

Here are the top marquee men – if they don’t come to terms with their incumbent clubs beforehand – that will be testing their market value. Nathan Cleary (Penrith Panthers) This is the biggest domino to fall in the transfer market. Undoubtedly the best and most influential player in the NRL, which will make Cleary’s the most sought-after signature in the game. The horrific leg injury suffered in the preliminary final is a curveball that nobody saw coming, but that won’t deter Penrith or other clubs from trying to secure his services. Walker said on Saturday his intention was to remain at the Roosters, though it remains to be seen if the club will budge on the initial extension offer his management declined to take up. title: Jealousy, friendship and love take centre-stage in this story
text:
Advertisement

Key points THEATRE: Eric Jiang’s Rhomboid has its Melbourne premiere at fortyfivedownstairs

OPERA: The Spare Room by Helen Garner has its world premiere

JAZZ: Za Górami put on a five-star show at MPAC Sound Gallery

THEATRE: Eliza at Southbank Theatre is a psychological thriller

THEATRE: Koreaboo at Malthouse draws from lived experience

THEATRE

Rhomboid ★★★★

fortyfivedownstairs, until October 11 Heartfelt, funny and sexy. Eric Jiang’s Rhomboid beautifully captures the ambiguity of platonic and romantic love through the orbiting lives of Xavier (Ken Paolo) and Sebastian (Lawrence Hawkins). Chad Rosete, Lawrence Hawkins and Ken Paolo. George Jefford From high school through to the onset of their careers, Xavier and Sebastian have been trying to figure out what they mean to each other. As they get older, and other paramours enter their lives — the introduction of supporting actor Chad Rosete, who plays both Xavier’s casual hook-up Lachie and Sebastian’s serious partner Felix— their relationship becomes murky and untethered.

Advertisement

The chemistry between the cast is fantastic, and the dialogue is pithy and fast-paced, with pop culture references woven in. This doesn’t take away from the emotional depth of the story, as they delve into jealousy, queer identity and the unevenness that can exist in friendships and love. Sebastian candidly admits that he “loves being the only Asian in a white crew”, and that he feels threatened by other Asian queers who are “more successful, smarter or hotter” than him. Lawrence Hawkins and Ken Paolo as Sebastian and Xavier. George Jefford The set (by Amy Todd) is simple and flexible: a tower of blocks looms in the centre, assembled like Tetris. The actors move the blocks between scenes to transform into a club, a station, an art gallery, a mountain for hiking, or a wedding, with simple yet effective changes to lighting, blocking and sound. The shifting of time between scenes is seamless, as gentle instrumental piano plays and a moving scene is projected, as if peering out the windows of a car on a highway, onto the blocks.

Advertisement

Margot Morales’ direction shines through in these choices, setting up the story like it’s a New York City-set indie rom-com; even the lead photo for the show positions Sebastian and Xavier on a steel stairwell between two brick buildings. Related Article Arts Three titans of politics, sport and media had a meeting in the 1980s. A new play imagines what was said The space is used well. When Sebastian is drunk, dancing erratically on his own in the club in the corner, and Xavier spots him from across the room out of the corner of his eye while dancing with Lachie, you can feel the tension and awkwardness. In scenes depicting text message exchanges, the characters are positioned apart across the blocks, facing away from each other and speaking out loud. The only critique is that it is a little long; tightening the script and scene choices would make the already strong material even punchier. A scene between three characters overexplains the significance of the rhomboid and feels clunky; the show is at its best when it leans into innuendo and subtext. Nonetheless, it was refreshing to witness theatre that centres queer young people unapologetically, without the usual trappings of a coming-out story. At the end, we’re left with this lingering thought: love isn’t clear-cut like a square — it’s angular and leaning like a rhomboid, changing and shifting with the passage of time.

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar

Advertisement

OPERA

The Spare Room ★★★★

Playhouse, until October 10 If you’re familiar with Helen Garner’s 2008 book, The Spare Room, you might think: how on earth could this be made into an opera? The Spare Room by Helen Garner has been adapted into an opera. Jeff Busby A semi-autobiographical meditation on what it is to care for someone who is dying, to put your own beliefs aside and support them indiscriminately, the book is visceral about the awfulness of cancer. The pain, the sweat, the pissing the bed. Levity is long gone. Composer Jane Hammond and her longtime collaborator, librettist Therèsa Borg, however, saw The Spare Room as ripe for the operatic picking.

Advertisement

With Garner’s blessing, a gestational process of almost five years ensued, finally resulting in Victorian Opera’s latest world premiere. It is a remarkable achievement, and it would be remiss not to mention: the author, composer, librettist, director, conductor, the two star performers and CEO of the company are all women. Natalie Jones and Antoinette Halloran star in The Spare Room. Jeff Busby In contemporary chamber style, Hammond has scored for 13 players, who here manage tiny moments of introspection and huge emotional outbursts. Bach is mentioned often in Garner’s text, and Hammond deftly weaves in some of the Three-Part Inventions, creating a gloriously layered amalgamation of styles and colours. Some of the magic is lost, however, in the amplification of voices and certain instruments, particularly percussion, which threw out the balance at times. Mic-ing opera singers means that, for the most part, there is no vocal light and shade, and we are left longing for some pianissimo.

Advertisement

As Helen, Natalie Jones is grounded and direct, with steely vocals that, suitably, border on shrill when the situation calls for it. Opposite Jones is Antoinette Halloran, perfectly cast as the woo-woo Nicola. Halloran still has such electric presence and the most magnificent stage face, and Nicola’s more expansive music suits Halloran’s lyric voice. Related Article Performing arts Helen Garner on the worst three weeks of her life The work itself gets better as the night progresses, and when the drama matches the book in its level of intensity. The confrontation between Helen and Nicola is extraordinary. Your enjoyment of this opera might depend on how wedded you are to Garner. There are moments of comedy, perhaps required for a two-hour stage adaptation, but do not align with the original text. There is a sense of belonging in seeing one’s own experience on stage. Cancer has touched almost everyone, and amid a very Melbourne staging, where there are comments about the weather, people riding bikes, this very masthead used as a prop – it’s validating to see women’s anxieties and naturalistic experiences presented in this heightened art form.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies

Advertisement

JAZZ

Za Górami ★★★★★

MPAC Sound Gallery, October 8 Za górami is a Polish expression meaning “behind the mountains”, often used to begin fairytales (akin to “Once upon a time”). It’s also the name of a much-loved Polish folk song – one that served as the title track and thematic anchor for the 2024 debut album by Alice Zawadzki, Fred Thomas and Misha Mullov-Abbado. Misha Mullov-Abbado, Alice Zawadzki and Fred Thomas. Monika Jakubowska The UK trio have now adopted Za Górami as their collective moniker, and it couldn’t be more apt. Each tune in their repertoire is a short story in musical form, its narrative gently unfurling while carrying echoes of faraway places and centuries-old cultures. Monash University’s David Li Sound Gallery provided a wonderfully intimate setting for Za Górami’s concert in Melbourne, its pristine acoustics allowing every detail of the trio’s interactions to be heard with absolute clarity.

Advertisement

Alice Zawadzki arrived on stage barefoot, warmly greeting the audience before beckoning us into a hushed Argentinian tale of hidden love. As the trio’s music draws heavily from European, Latin and Sephardic Jewish folk sources, Zawadzki sang mostly in foreign languages and dialects: Spanish, French, Sardinian, Ladino. But the expressiveness of her voice and gestures – coupled with the subtle but exquisite musical arrangements – helped convey the poetry of the lyrics and the sentiments within them. Fred Thomas (on piano and drums) and Misha Mullov-Abbado (bass) are both masters of understatement, able to suggest emotional undercurrents with the flick of a brush, a lightly tapped cymbal or a shiver of bowed-bass harmonics. On Je Suis Trop Jeunette, Thomas rubbed a mallet across the piano strings to underline the delicacy of Zawadzki’s wistful lyrics; then the mood darkened, with emphatic chords and bass scampering beneath the singer’s soaring wordless explorations. Several tunes also featured Zawadzki’s violin – lightly plucked and effervescent, or gracefully harmonising with her elegant vocal lines. The final tune even included animal sound effects (courtesy of the audience, whinnying and neighing on command), adding an air of whimsy to this entrancing evening of musical storytelling.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas

Advertisement

THEATRE

Eliza ★★★★★

Southbank Theatre, The Sumner until October 31 Prognoses of AI’s impact upon humanity has reached fever pitch, but in Tom Holloway’s play, we are catapulted into the past to grapple with the very same questions we’re seeking answers to 60 years later. Dan Spielman (left) and Manali Datar in Eliza. Pia Johnson Dr Joseph Weizenbaum (Dan Spielman) is a mercurial visiting professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, as intent on repressing the traumatic memories of his escape from Nazi Germany as he is on heralding the advent of digital computers. When his secretary, Becky (a bewitching Manali Datar) makes a seemingly inconsequential joke about the back-and-forth cadence of talk therapy, it opens the doors to the creation of the world’s first chatbot: Eliza.

Advertisement

The breathtaking scale of invention is mirrored in the expansiveness of Dale Ferguson’s vertiginous set. Rows upon rows of systematically aligned towers of working files and cascading sheets of glass lend an unexplainable depth and dimension to the stage, creating rabbit warrens for the characters to lose themselves in as their sense of reality and personhood begin to blur. The play traces the ethical quandaries inherent in AI back to its genesis. Weizenbaum is shown to be well-meaning, but his disavowal of personal disclosure, refusal to listen until it’s too late and his betrayal of Becky, in particular, is a recurring theme that can be extrapolated to AI’s routine, large-scale copyright thefts in the present day. Although set in the 1960s, Eliza raises philosophical and ethical concerns about the role of AI in society. Pia Johnson The famed sycophancy of AI that is leading to current crises of consciousness is shown to have had very much the same effect when it was conceived in the 1960s, as people yearned to unburden themselves to what they perceived to be a neutral entity. Under Paige Rattray’s direction, the rapid-fire play unfurls at the brisk pace of a psychological thriller as a collective psychosis and breakdown of legibility takes hold of the characters in different ways, as they talk around one another without truly understanding each other.

Advertisement

This strange incomprehension finds its expression in the motif of starlings, which is, incidentally, the namesake of a company spying on Weizenbaum’s exploits. Related Article Arts Culture wars and a swing to the right: A new take on Gone With the Wind is coming Through spectacular audiovisual mastery and a stunning Hitchcockian reckoning, the forward march of progress is disturbingly realised in increasingly absurd and surreal ways as Weizenbaum figuratively and literally chokes on the irreversible weight of what he has set in motion. Spielman excels as the fulcrum, superbly marrying the constant whirring of a beautiful mind with an inexplicable childlike naivete. Datar’s transition from unknowing to seemingly all-knowing in a role that Holloway resurrected from the annals of history is chilling, and there isn’t a role that Hamish Michael can’t play, as he dovetails seamlessly between aggrieved research assistant, enthused journalist and lofty powers that be. The philosophical and ethical concerns that Eliza raises are by no means new to anyone engaged in the broader debate around AI, but in this undidactic, morally nuanced play, the inextricability of latent humanity and technological advancement is laid bare once more.

Reviewed by Sonia Nair

Advertisement

JAZZ

Julian Banks Quartet ★★★★

Cross St Music Hall, October 2 Almost a decade after releasing his previous album, saxophonist Julian Banks has brought his latest album to life in a rush of inspiration and energy. The Julian Banks Quartet performed at Cross Street Music Hall on Friday, October 2. Leila Maulen Just four months after recording the new material, here it was: available on CD and launched on Friday night with an exuberant live performance at the Cross Street Music Hall. The convivial Brunswick venue was the perfect place to hear this music. The tunes Banks writes – like the rooms at Cross Street – are warm, inviting and innately appealing without trying to impress.

Advertisement

The new album, OxyMoron, celebrates Banks’ renewed passion for playing and performing his own music after navigating various life challenges in recent years, and is imbued with a positive spirit that a live setting amplified. This gig clearly meant a lot to the saxophonist, and every phrase that emerged from his tenor was filled with feeling. His marvellously rich tone magnified the soulful allure of his melodies and added muscular vigour to his solos. Saxophonist Julian Banks has released his first album in a decade. Leila Maulen His bandmates (guitarist Louis King, bassist James Gilligan and drummer Joe Talia) gathered beside rather than behind him, reflecting their role as equal contributors in this enterprise. King’s electric guitar could float in a fuzzy haze or bite into a distortion-laden solo; Gilligan’s semi-acoustic bass guitar was by turns sinuous and insistent; and Talia conjured up languid shuffles and headily propulsive grooves with effortless ease.

Advertisement

Captain Happy skipped nimbly between shifting time signatures, while the album’s title track saw the band veering into crunchy rock territory without losing the sense of warmth or approachability that characterises Banks’ music. Perhaps the night’s most affecting piece was Little Dove – a ballad dedicated to Banks’ young daughter, whose burgeoning love of music helped reignite Banks’ passion for his own, and who sat proudly in the front row at the launch.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas THEATRE

Koreaboo ★★★

Malthouse, until October 10 Inspired by playwright Michelle Lim Davidson’s own experiences and directed by Jessica Arthur, Koreaboo is a two-hander that surveys contentious issues of race, diaspora and belonging, with a light touch. Heather Jeong (left) and Michelle Lim Davidson in a scene from Koreaboo. Gianna Rizzo

Advertisement

Davidson herself plays Hannah, a young Australian who travels to Seoul in an attempt to reconnect with her estranged birth mother, Umma (Heather Jeong). It’s only their second meeting. We learn that although she was born in South Korea, Hannah was adopted as a baby and grew up in Newcastle, NSW. At the start, the two women fail and flail in communication. Hannah was expecting a summer-long stay – a long enough period, perhaps, for meaningful reconnection; Umma (mother in Korean), however, believed it was just going to be a short vacation. The two women in Koreaboo fail and flail in communication. Gianna Rizzo Umma’s behaviour toward her daughter thrums with wariness, as though one were greeting a stranger. Maybe, she suggests, Hannah should be visiting Seoul’s touristy spots instead. The entire performance is staged in a small convenience store run by Umma, lovingly decked out in all manner of brightly coloured snacks, and with harsh fluorescent lighting thanks to designer Mel Page. The two women move within the space as they interrogate, parry and deflect.

Advertisement

Davidson explores a raft of issues, including the question of identity. Hannah’s hyphenated background (Korean-Australian) means she’s part of both cultures and wholly of neither, and at first, Umma’s brusque criticism of Hannah’s language skills feels like a wholesale rejection of her daughter’s “Koreanness”. Seeking both maternal and cultural acceptance, Hannah feels crushed to receive neither. Related Article Performing arts Star of ABC hit The Newsreader mines real-life family drama for new project Their common language – and one that helps them move toward connection and bridge distance, it turns out – is K-pop. The title actually refers to someone who’s not of Korean heritage but who is obsessed with Korean pop culture. Koreaboo swerves to the unexpected and surreal when both performers begin to sing and dance. There is a talent show in the offing to prepare for, and a chance for Hannah to become more Korean. It’s all surface-level cultural appropriation, though, much in the same way that Umma learnt English by watching TV, becoming so familiar with the lives of the characters in Sex and the City that she can quote from them. After a shaky start, Jeong and Davidson become good sparring partners and friends as they navigate the tricky mother-daughter relationship anew after years apart. Umma’s backstory is revealed: the reasons behind Hannah’s adoption and how her yearnings for a singing career were quashed because of filial obedience to her own mother. Korean culture is not just skincare and pop music, but, like a lot of Asian countries, there’s an expectation to conform to parental demands.

Advertisement

Koreaboo packs in a lot during its 90-minute stage time – maybe too much, as there is a lot of jumping about trying to cover a lot of ground. The beginning set-up takes a while to develop and can be tightened, and the ending feels rushed. And although the singing and dance sequences are overextended and as distracting as they are humorous, the play’s value is drawn from highlighting the possible consequences of adopting a child, removing them from their motherland, and raising them in an entirely foreign environment. Even if they embrace the riches of a new life in their host country, there are always losses to be reckoned with.

Reviewed by Thuy On OPERA

The Turn of the Screw ★★★

Palais Theatre, until October 1 Operatic takes on the supernatural span the centuries, but no modern work is more revered and feared than Benjamin Britten’s The Turn of the Screw. The 1954 opera follows a governess who takes up residence at an English country house, only to find the spirits of two dead servants are haunting the children now in her care. From left: Rachelle Durkin, Genevieve Gray and Oliver Thadoe Naing in The Turn of the Screw. Jeff Busby

Advertisement

Finally, an opera where the muffled screams drifting in from Luna Park next door actually add to the drama, rather than detract! This is a piece that has potential to be The Shining-level unnerving. When staged up close and creepy, the eerie singing and sinister spectacle can captivate like a demonic spirit itself. Here, the huge set and vast stage dwarf the drama – in pivotal moments, the singers are far away from each other; we are far away from them. Detachment creates a disconnect that does not serve some excellent performances. Durkin, Michaela Cadwgan and Kanen Breen in The Turn of the Screw. Jeff Busby It is, after all, a chamber opera. Britten scored it for just 13 instruments. Perhaps no Australian conductor knows more about the English composer than Paul Kildea, and the reduced Orchestra Victoria was guided superbly by him. Rachelle Durkin (Governess) was more maternal than hysterical, with a self-assured, impressive vocal performance to match. Kanen Breen’s voice is sharp and cold and uses his lithe physicality to intensify Peter Quint’s menace, despite donning the most unflattering wig anyone’s ever been cursed to wear (it’s a confusing choice, when it’s clearly mentioned how handsome Quint is).

Advertisement

One exceptional discovery to come from this production is soprano Genevieve Gray (currently a university student), who sings the older child, Flora. Gray possesses a vocal evenness and an array of colour that belies her youth. Neither a spook nor a snore, though with moments of satisfaction, this production feels like a missed opportunity to bewitch more people with the mystery and magic of operatic storytelling.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies MUSIC

Lady Blackbird ★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, September 30 It’s been decades since Lady Blackbird – raised in an evangelical Christian household in New Mexico – abandoned her church-music roots, along with the religious doctrines that no longer defined her. Singer Lady Blackbird.

Advertisement

These days, the message underpinning her music is much more personal, but no less spiritually charged. The American singer (born Marley Munroe) has a voice to rival any gospel queen, but it’s now self-empowerment and self-acceptance she champions, rather than submission to an external force. In Melbourne on Wednesday, as part of her debut Australian tour, Lady Blackbird cut a striking figure as she arrived on stage: floor-sweeping black dress, elegant cane and signature platinum afro. Her three-piece band (guitarist Chris Seefried, bassist Jonathan Flaugher and Melbourne drummer Felix Bloxsom) stoked a gritty, distortion-flecked fire around the singer for Pink Floyd’s Mother, then retreated to the shadows for Blackbird, the haunting Nina Simone song that inspired the singer’s stage moniker. Related Article Melbourne live reviews This haunting play celebrates the solidarity and strangeness of found family On Collage, the amped-up fuzz of electric bass and guitar magnified the drama but almost submerged Blackbird’s glorious vocals. Then the mood softened – first with the addition of acoustic bass, then acoustic guitar. This was Blackbird in heartfelt confessional mode, her gorgeously grainy voice brimming with emotion on a clutch of originals: the soulfully swaying Lost and Looking, the jazz-tinted Five Feet Tall and the lilting, folky Man on a Boat. Seefried switched to piano for the wistful If I Told You before ushering in another cloud of psychedelia on a heady rendition of The Beatles’ Come Together. Blackbird’s musical world is unconstrained by genre, and her emotional commitment and authenticity allow her to make each song her own, whether it was written by her or others.

Advertisement

Imaginative arrangements and reharmonisations also allow the audience to hear old songs with fresh ears. In Blackbird’s hands, Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door became a hushed torch song, exquisitely understated. Her spellbinding encore – I Am What I Am – was equally unadorned, stripped of its Broadway sequins to become a quietly defiant affirmation of identity.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

Boom recruit Zak Butters says the Western Bulldogs are on the cusp of “something special”, and revealed he turned to Marcus Bontempelli for advice throughout the year before making his decision to head to the Whitten Oval. Butters, 26, is officially a Bulldog on a record nine-year contract worth between $17 million and $17.5 million after the AFL on Friday approved a convoluted side deal involving five clubs and a series of first, second and later draft picks exchanged. The Butters contract is the biggest in AFL history in total, though he will earn less than the $2 million per season St Kilda’s Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera has made. Ready to start: Zak Butters is looking forward to getting to work with the Western Bulldogs. And I felt like, yeah, once I knew, I just wanted to get it done, and get here and meet everyone and start my next journey.” Butters had already formed a friendship with Bontempelli, the Bulldogs’ skipper and legendary figure, which the club had felt was a factor in their favour in the intense competition for the midfield gun that also involved Richmond and Geelong. “He’s obviously one that I am looking forward to playing with, and he’s been an inspiration of mine since I was a kid, and probably more so the more I got to know him, not just this year, but along the journey and playing against him,” Butters told the Bulldogs’ website. “[I’m] trying to be the best, so you’re trying to learn off the best, and he’s he’s definitely one of them. He played for the Western Jets before being taken by the Power with the 12th pick of the 2018 national draft. He said one of the highlights of his life had been attending the 2016 finals, when the Bulldogs unexpectedly stormed to their second club premiership. “Yeah, I have loved the Bulldogs since I was a kid, had plenty of jumpers growing up, and loved a lot of different players. But, probably, 2016 is hard to top,” Butters said.

“I remember catching the train in from Bacchus Marsh, and watching the finals, and was lucky enough to sneak a few tickets through friends and family. And yeah, I remember catching the train home after the ’16 granny [grand final], and, obviously, catching the train back through the west to get to Bacchus Marsh, it was pretty chaotic and loud. “It’s still one of my favourite days that I’ve had in footy. So it’d be cool to try and run that back.” Butters said he wants to be role model for youth in the western suburbs, reinforcing that they, too, can reach the heights of elite football.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
